Two things live here, and they are the two halves of one loop.

**Papers.** Finished write-ups, produced with the help of AI and put through [review](/reviews/index.qmd) before their status advances. No restriction is placed on how much of the work the AI did: what is graded is what has been checked, not who or what produced it. That is the whole basis on which this section differs from a conventional venue, and the argument for it is on the [Philosophy](/philosophy/index.qmd) page.

**Proposals.** Open-ended research projects, written in the spirit of a grant proposal rather than a result: a question worth attacking, why it is tractable now, and what a serious attempt would involve. A proposal is an invitation to develop it with AI assistance and publish the outcome here as a paper. That is the loop, and the reason proposals sit beside the archive rather than in a separate corner of the site.

A paper need not resolve a conjecture posted under [Problems](/problems/index.qmd). It may settle some other cryptographic question, one of wider interest without being tracked here as an open statement, and it may take several forms: a precise write-up of a new result, an expository account or tutorial, a systematization of existing knowledge, or work that makes a known result more rigorous by closing a gap in a proof or tightening its statement.

Each paper carries a status badge in the same style as a conjecture's, for now graded at the level of the whole paper (its statement, proof, and Lean formalization if any). Grading individual theorems within a paper separately, once a paper has several worth distinguishing, is a natural next step, not something done yet.

This kind of work has always mattered and has always been undersupplied, because there is little professional reward for writing a clear tutorial, consolidating scattered results, or painstakingly re-checking someone else's proof: the incentives point toward new results, not toward the unglamorous scholarship that consolidates and secures them. What has changed is the cost. AI makes this kind of careful, precise write-up cheap enough to do routinely rather than occasionally, which is exactly why it belongs on a site like this.

## Archive

Every paper on Conjura is listed on the [Archive](/projects/archive/index.qmd) page. Each carries a [status badge](/problems/status-legend/index.qmd) graded on the same scale as a conjecture's: what has been checked, by whom, and how, and never more than that. A paper being listed there says it exists and is addressable, not that it is finished.

[Browse the Archive →](/projects/archive/index.qmd)

## Proposals

A proposal names a focused research topic — narrower than a survey, not yet precise enough to be a conjecture — that an AI (possibly multi-agent, possibly distributed) works by surveying the literature, generating and checking candidate statements, and autoformalizing whatever holds up. The result seeds a paper in the [Archive](/projects/archive/index.qmd) or an [open problem](/problems/index.qmd). Proposals exist for people with the idea but not the compute to pursue it themselves; posting one is how it gets worked anyway, by whoever picks it up.

A proposal comes from one of two provenances: a **submitted** proposal is a fresh idea someone posts directly; a **harvested** proposal is a direction a paper's own future-work section already names, found and quoted the same way a conjecture is, but rejected by the conjecture harvester for lacking a single provable claim. Rejection by that pipeline isn't a defect in the paper — posing a direction rather than a claim is a normal, common thing for a paper to do, and a harvested proposal is where that outcome goes instead of being discarded.

A paper that already has a promoted conjecture on this site can still contribute a proposal — a conjecture is one precise claim a paper poses; a proposal is a different, vaguer direction the same paper names elsewhere. They aren't competing descriptions of the same gap.

Every open proposal carries one or more topic tags, StackExchange-style; browse them grouped by tag on the [By Topic](/projects/proposals/by-topic/index.qmd) page.

[Browse open proposals →](/projects/proposals/index.qmd)
